Memory and HBM

SK hynix, Samsung and Micron make nearly all high bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked memory beside AI chips. SK hynix took 63.2 percent of HBM revenue in 2025.

Memory and HBM, stage 10 of 15Next stage: 11 Advanced Packaging

In plain terms

High bandwidth memory, or HBM, is where an AI chip keeps the numbers it is working on, and it is built to hand them over fast. A memory maker etches tiny holes into each memory wafer, fills them with copper and grinds the wafer until the copper shows through its back. It tests each of the wafer's chips and stacks up to sixteen good ones into a cube, with every layer wired to the ones below. The cube then sits beside the processor, the chip that does the calculating. Stacking is the hard part because each chip is ground thinner than a human hair and the finished cube has to stay within a set height. One chip that fails after stacking can scrap the whole cube. Only SK hynix, Samsung and Micron make HBM in volume, and a single entry in the US export rules covers HBM from all three.

In short

US-based Micron went from 5.8 percent of HBM revenue in 2024 to 23.1 percent in the first quarter of 2026[13]. Over the same period, Samsung's share fell from 37.8 percent to 20.5 percent[13].

Since December 2024, a US license has been required, unless an exception applies, to export to China any HBM moving more than 2 GB per second per square millimeter of its area[1]. The Institute for Progress reported in October 2025 that China's CXMT planned to produce HBM3 in 2026[22]. Even so, the institute estimated that the United States and its partners would make 70 times as much HBM as China in 2026[22].

Why substitution is slow
A fourth maker would find it hard to break in. It would need the newest DRAM, a line that drills through and thins wafers, and a way to stack the thinned chips without warping them, all inside one company. Its stack would then have to pass a customer's qualification tests.
Where China stands

The Institute for Progress estimated in October 2025 that China would make virtually no HBM that year. Huawei said in September 2025 that its Ascend 950 chips would use two HBM designs of its own, without saying who would manufacture the memory.

Where the US stands

Micron is the only American HBM maker. License Exception HBM lets exporters headquartered in the United States or a Country Group A:5 ally ship HBM below 3.3 GB per second per square millimeter without a license.

See it in 3D in the interactive chapter

An AI accelerator moves numbers from memory to its arithmetic units and back. The cost of arithmetic has fallen faster than the cost of moving numbers. The US export control office wrote in December 2024 that a processor cannot reach its full capabilities unless its memory capacity and bandwidth rise with its speed[1].

How it works

Each layer in the cube is a DRAM chip, the ordinary kind of computer memory. Each layer is ground thin and bonded to the one below through tiny metal bumps called microbumps. The whole stack sits on a base die, a chip that manages it. The copper-filled holes are called through-silicon vias, or TSVs. They let a signal reach any layer without a wire running around the outside.

An HBM3E cube has a 1,024-bit interface, meaning it exchanges data with the processor over 1,024 wires at once[2]. That is sixteen times wider than a standard DDR5 memory module, the memory stick in a PC[2]. HBM4 doubles that to 2,048 wires[3]. Ordinary memory cannot be made that wide, because the pins would not fit on a circuit board. The stack can, since its wires run down through the TSVs and across a silicon interposer to the processor beside it, with no board in the way[2].

A chip needs the width most when it answers a prompt. Training reuses each stored number across a huge multiplication, so a chip can fetch little and compute a lot. But to generate one word of an answer, the chip reads the whole model from memory, plus the whole record of the conversation so far. Then it does a little arithmetic and waits for the next read. That record grows with the length of the conversation and the number of users served at once. So memory size and speed usually set how many people one chip can serve.

HBM3E

Micron's HBM3E comes in two sizes, 24 GB with eight chips stacked and 36 GB with twelve[4]. SK hynix's January 2026 market outlook says major research and brokerage analysts expect HBM3E to be about two thirds of all HBM shipments in 2026[5].

HBM4

The standards body JEDEC published JESD270-4 in April 2025, setting the 2,048-bit interface and 2 TB/s per stack at 8 Gb/s per pin[3]. SK hynix says it was first to complete HBM4 development, in September 2025, at over 10 Gb/s per pin[6]. Samsung says it began mass production and shipped the first commercial HBM4 in February 2026, at 11.7 Gb/s per pin, with a 4 nm logic base die[7]. Micron's parts run above 11 Gb/s for more than 2.8 TB/s per stack[8].

Through HBM3E, SK hynix made its own base dies, the chips at the bottom of each stack[9]. For HBM4 it chose TSMC's advanced logic process, so the base die can hold more functions[9]. As a result, TSMC, which does not make HBM, makes the base die for SK hynix's HBM4.

How a stack is built

  • Drill and thin. Etch vertical holes, the through-silicon vias, into a memory wafer, fill them with copper, then grind the wafer from behind until the copper comes through.
  • Stack and join. Thermocompression bonding joins the chips through metal bumps under heat and pressure, and it comes in several forms[11]. SK hynix uses Advanced MR-MUF, which stacks the chips, injects a liquid protective material between them and hardens it[6]. SK hynix says the process controls warping and dissipates heat well[6]. Samsung said in February 2024 that its twelve-high HBM3E uses TC-NCF, thermocompression with a thin non-conductive film between the chips[12]. Samsung expected TC-NCF to help limit warping as chips get thinner[12].
  • Stay under the height limit. HBM4 raised the package specification height of a finished cube from 720 micrometers to 775, still under a millimeter[11].

Hybrid bonding is the next step, but it is not ready. It would press copper pad straight onto copper pad, with no solder and no filler, and cut the spacing between connections from about 20 micrometers to under 1[11]. A tech note on SK hynix's newsroom says full-scale adoption in HBM is most likely at HBM4E or HBM5, where stacks are projected to pass twenty layers[11]. Heat builds up in the stack, and removing it becomes a major challenge at 16 to 20 layers[11].

Who makes it

Three firms took more than 90 percent of the revenue from ordinary computer memory, or DRAM, in the first quarter of 2026[13]. HBM comes from the same three, SK hynix, Samsung and Micron[13]. No other company has both leading-edge DRAM and a stacking line of its own.

SK hynix was the first company to mass-produce several generations of HBM, including HBM3 and HBM3E[13]. UBS, as quoted in SK hynix's January 2026 market outlook, expected SK hynix to take about 70 percent of the HBM4 market for Nvidia's Rubin platform in 2026[5].

SK hynix broke ground in August 2026 on an advanced packaging plant in West Lafayette, Indiana, an investment of over $4 billion[14]. Micron is modernizing its DRAM and HBM production capacity in Taiwan[15]. It has also broken ground on an HBM advanced packaging plant in Singapore to expand its packaging capacity from 2027[15].

Of 2025 HBM revenue, SK hynix took 63.2 percent, Samsung 19.3 and Micron 17.4[13]. The split is public because SK hynix registered shares in the United States[13]. Its US prospectus credits the research firm IDC. Market shares move fast. In 2024 the same three stood at 56.4, 37.8 and 5.8 percent[13]. In the first quarter of 2026 they stood at 56.4, 20.5 and 23.1 percent[13].

Bank of America, in an estimate SK hynix quoted in January 2026, put the 2026 HBM market at $54.6 billion, up 58 percent on 2025[5]. SK hynix says HBM needs more wafers than traditional DRAM, the kind used in PCs and phones[13]. It also says the industry's shift of production capacity to HBM has left traditional DRAM undersupplied[13]. The shortage, it says, helped drive a significant price recovery for that DRAM from the third quarter of 2025[13].

The chokepoint

Every leading accelerator made outside China depends on Korean or American HBM. Nvidia's GB300 NVL72 rack carries 20 TB of HBM3E at up to 576 TB/s[16]. Each Nvidia Rubin GPU carries up to 288 GB of HBM4 at up to 22 TB/s[17]. AMD's MI355X carries 288 GB of HBM3E at 8 TB/s[18].

On 5 December 2024 the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the US export control office, published a rule at 89 FR 96790. It added an export classification, ECCN 3A090.c, for "High bandwidth memory (HBM) having a 'memory bandwidth density' greater than 2 gigabytes per second per square millimeter". Its technical note defines that density as the memory bandwidth in gigabytes per second divided by the area of the package or stack in square millimeters. The rule also covers stacks made outside the United States, through a foreign direct product rule, which applies US controls to goods made abroad with American technology[1]. BIS stated in the rule that all HBM stacks then in production exceeded that threshold[1].

Under 15 CFR 742.6(b)(10)(ii), BIS reviews license applications to send 3A090.c items to Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination such as China[19]. It reviews them with a presumption of approval when neither the buyer nor its ultimate parent is headquartered in one of those places, and with a presumption of denial otherwise[19].

Two provisions narrow the control. License Exception HBM, at 15 CFR 740.25, applies to exporters headquartered in the United States or a Country Group A:5 ally[20]. It lets them ship HBM below 3.3 GB per second per square millimeter without a license[20]. The HBM must be bought directly by the designer of the chip it will be packaged into and must go straight to the packaging site[20]. The rule also excludes co-packaged chips that combine HBM and logic and whose main function is processing, which other chip controls may cover instead[1].

The think tank CSIS said in December 2024 that the rules still allowed HBM2 to go to China with end-use and end-user restrictions[21]. It also said Nvidia's H20, whose HBM3 is packaged with the processor, was then still exportable under the accelerator thresholds[21].

In December 2024 CSIS called China's strongest DRAM maker, CXMT, one of only two Chinese firms with a credible path to producing advanced HBM[21]. The Institute for Progress reported in October 2025 that CXMT was planning to produce HBM3 in 2026[22]. It also estimated that China would make virtually no HBM in 2025[22]. Huawei said in September 2025 that its Ascend 950 chips would use two HBM designs of its own, HiBL 1.0 and HiZQ 2.0[23]. It said the 950DT, due in the fourth quarter of 2026, would carry 144 GB of HiZQ 2.0 at 4 TB/s[23]. The announcement did not say who would manufacture the memory[23]. SK hynix says HBM needs advanced production processes, such as TSV packaging, and must pass the rigorous testing and approval processes its customers set[13].

Review questions

Open a question to see its answer.

What is HBM?

High-bandwidth memory, made of memory chips stacked into a cube beside the processor and wired to pass data fast.

Before stacking, each chip gets holes filled with copper, which wire every layer to the ones below. A stack holds up to sixteen chips. Reread: How it works

Why does an AI chip need such fast memory?

For each word it writes, it reads the whole model from memory.

Memory speed and size usually set how many users one chip can serve. Reread: How it works

Who makes HBM?

SK hynix, Samsung and Micron make nearly all of it.

SK hynix sold 63.2 percent of it in 2025 and Samsung 19.3 percent. A fourth maker would need both the newest DRAM, the kind of memory chip used in PCs and phones, and a line that stacks it. Reread: Who makes it

Can China get advanced HBM?

Not the newest kinds, and no Chinese firm ships HBM3E or HBM4 in volume.

Since December 2024, US controls have covered HBM above 2 GB per second per square millimeter, and BIS, the US export control office, said every stack then in production crossed that line. A license exception lets stacks below 3.3 GB per second per square millimeter ship without a license if they go straight to the chip designer's packaging site. HBM already packaged with a processor, as on Nvidia's H20, falls under the chip rules instead. Reread: The chokepoint
